claims.text: Atomic-scale disorder can produce a uniform, single-phase microstructure in a lightweight high-entropy alloy.
A uniform disordered solid solution provides solid-solution strengthening.
A uniform single-phase microstructure favors formation of a coherent, slow-growing protective oxide scale.
Microsegregation or secondary-phase precipitation compromises strengthening and protective-oxide mechanisms.
Slower cooling or annealing can induce microsegregation or secondary-phase precipitation in the alloy.
A uniform disordered alloy structure limits diffusion.
Diffusion limitation increases yield strength and slows oxidation and corrosion.
Microsegregation creates localized regions of reduced strength.
Microsegregation makes protective barrier formation less effective.
Microsegregation creates accelerated diffusion pathways that increase corrosion and oxidation.
The homogeneous baseline alloy will have higher yield strength than the microsegregated variant under identical test conditions.
The homogeneous baseline alloy will have a lower corrosion rate than the microsegregated variant.
The homogeneous baseline alloy will exhibit lower high-temperature oxidation mass gain than the microsegregated variant.
The performance difference may vanish when microsegregation is too slight to affect microstructure-dependent properties.
Precipitates below a threshold size may not significantly influence diffusion or produce a performance difference.
At sufficiently extreme temperatures, oxidation kinetics may overwhelm the proposed microstructure-dependent protective mechanism.
